blocks.text: Here's the trap almost every performance marketer falls into. ROAS looks fine, so you leave the campaign alone. Then one morning ROAS drops off a cliff and you scramble to react. But ROAS is a lagging indicator — by the time it falls, the fatigue that caused it has been building for a week or more. You're not catching the problem; you're catching the aftermath.
The marketers who stay efficient have learned to read the leading signals — the ones that move 48 hours into fatigue, not 10 days into it. Here they are, with the thresholds that matter.
What ad fatigue actually is

Ad fatigue happens when the same people see the same creative too many times. Novelty wears off, the creative becomes wallpaper, response rates fall — and the algorithm, trying to keep delivering, pushes your ad to less and less responsive segments of the audience, which makes everything worse. It's a compounding decline, which is exactly why early detection pays off so much: a small intervention early prevents a large collapse later.

blocks.text: Crucially, the decline starts in the engagement metrics and only later reaches ROAS. That lag is your window. Miss it and you're refreshing after you've already overpaid.
The 4 early signals (and the thresholds)
No single metric is conclusive on its own — daily numbers are noisy. The signal is two or more of these moving together over several days.
Signal 1 — Frequency climbing past ~2.5

Frequency is average impressions per person. As it rises, each additional view does less work. A common practical threshold is around 2.5: below it you usually have room, above it fatigue risk rises sharply (the exact number varies by audience size, funnel stage, and creative). Frequency is the earliest warning because it predicts fatigue before performance even moves — it tells you saturation is coming.
Signal 2 — CTR dropping >20% week-over-week

Click-through rate is the cleanest read on whether the creative still earns attention. Compare this week to last week (not day to day — too noisy). A week-over-week CTR decline of more than ~20% on a creative whose audience hasn't changed is a strong fatigue signal. The audience is scrolling past what used to stop them.
Signal 3 — CPM rising on a stable audience

If your targeting hasn't changed but your cost per thousand impressions is climbing, the platform is effectively charging you more to reach the same people — often because your engagement-driven relevance is slipping. Rising CPM plus falling CTR is a classic fatigue fingerprint.
Signal 4 — CVR softening

Conversion rate is the closest leading signal to ROAS, so when it starts sliding, the ROAS drop is close behind. By the time CVR moves, fatigue is well underway — treat this as your "you're already late, act today" alarm rather than an early warning.
The 48-hour read
Put together, here's a simple daily check that takes two minutes:

items: Frequency above 2.5 and rising? Yellow flag — start preparing a refresh.
Is CTR down >20% vs last week? Red flag — fatigue is active.
CPM up on unchanged targeting? Confirms it.
CVR slipping? You're at the edge — refresh immediately.

blocks.text: The decision rule: when two of these move together for two-plus consecutive days, act. Don't wait for ROAS to confirm what the leading signals already told you — that confirmation costs you a week of inefficient spend.
What "refresh" should actually mean
Catching fatigue early is only useful if your response is ready. Refreshing doesn't mean panic-launching a random new ad — that just resets the clock without learning anything.

items: **Have variations queued before you need them.** The brands that respond to fatigue in hours, not days, already had the next creative built. Fatigue detection and a creative testing pipeline are two halves of the same system.
**Change the hook, not just the colors.** Most fatigue lives in the first three seconds. A new opening hook on the same offer often re-energizes performance more than a whole new concept.
**Rotate, don't just replace.** Cycling between a small set of proven creatives can extend the life of all of them by spreading frequency.

blocks.text: Watching four metrics across every active creative, every day, by hand is exactly the kind of monitoring that slips when you're busy — which is when fatigue does its damage. Automated alerting (the kind HypeOn surfaces) flags the two-signals-moving-together pattern so you intervene inside the 48-hour window instead of discovering it in next week's ROAS report.
This article discusses advertising performance metrics, not financial advice.

faq.a: Ad fatigue is when an audience has seen a creative so many times that they stop responding to it. Engagement and conversion rates fall, and because the algorithm keeps trying to deliver, performance compounds downward until ROAS drops.

faq.q: What frequency is too high for Meta ads?
faq.a: There's no universal number, but a frequency above roughly 2.5 is a common point where fatigue risk rises noticeably. The right threshold depends on audience size, funnel stage, and creative — treat 2.5 as a yellow flag to start watching closely, not a hard rule.

faq.q: How do I know if my ad is fatiguing before ROAS drops?
faq.a: Watch the leading signals: rising frequency, a week-over-week CTR drop greater than ~20%, CPM climbing on unchanged targeting, and softening conversion rate. When two or more move together for a couple of days, fatigue is active even if ROAS still looks fine.

faq.q: How often should I refresh creative?
faq.a: Refresh based on signals, not a fixed calendar. Some creatives fatigue in days at high spend; others last weeks. Monitor the four signals and refresh when they trip — and keep variations queued so you can act within 48 hours.
